Learning Objectives
Develop an awareness of the classification of congenital differences in the upper extremity.
Perform an appropriate workup of patients with congenital upper extremity differences.
Determine the surgical and nonsurgical treatment options for the management of congenital
upper extremity differences.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Congenital differences in the upper extremity vary greatly in presentation, severity of
expression, and resultant functional limitations.1,2


Overview
Congenital upper extremity differences is an umbrella term that includes various upper
extremity anomalies with different appearances and functional limitations. These upper
extremity deformities may occur in isolation or as part of a larger syndrome of
malformations involving other organ systems. Multidisciplinary care should be used to
manage all facets of the patient’s condition. Somes patients may be adequately treated
via observation alone, whereas other patients require complex reconstructive surgery to
allow for participation in normal daily activities and to limit the psychological effects of
growing up with an upper extremity deformity. Knowledge of the appropriate indications
and timing of surgical treatment is crucial for these patients because some conditions
require early management to prevent deficits in growth and development, with other
treatment options deferred until later stages of development.
Epidemiology
Data from the past 50 years show that the incidence of upper extremity anomalies is between
5.25 and 29.9 in 10,000 live births, with the prevalence ranging from 19.7 to 27.2 in 10,000 live
births.3-7
Approximately 10% of these patients have partial or total absence of the affected extremity,
causing substantial aesthetic and/or functional limitations.8
The most common conditions include syndactyly, polydactyly, congenital amputations,
camptodactyly, clinodactyly, brachydactyly, and radial longitudinal deficiency (RLD).9

The incidence and prevalence of congenital upper limb differences vary based on
ethnicity and geographic area. Birth registry studies from Scotland, Finland, and Sweden
reported that the incidence of upper limb anomalies ranges from 5 to 30 in 10,000 live
births. Studies from Western Australia and New York State reported prevalence rates
ranging from 20 to 27 in 10,000 live births.3-7Approximately 10% of affected infants have
substantial functional or aesthetic deficits.8 These conditions are more common in
males, preterm and post-term infants, multiple births, and advanced maternal age.10
The most common malformations of the hand plate include syndactyly and polydactyly,
and the most common malformations of the entire upper limb are transverse deficiency
and RLD.9,10
Embryology and Development
Embryology (Resource 1)
The limb bud first appears during the fourth week of gestation, with the upper limb
developing during weeks five to eight of gestation.
Several signaling centers are critical for upper limb development.
The apical ectodermal ridge is mediated by fibroblast growth factors and guides proximal-
to-distal development and interdigital apoptosis.
The zone of polarizing activity is mediated by sonic hedgehog growth factor and other
growth factors and guides anteroposterior (radioulnar) development.
Wnt signaling, which is mediated by the action of Wnt7a and other homeobox genes,
guides dorsoventral development.
Developmental milestones:
Highly variable
General guidelines are listed in Table 1
Radiographic appearance of secondary centers of ossification
Carpal bones ossify in a predictable sequence: capitate (3 to 4 months), hamate (4 to 8
months), triquetrum (2 to 3 years), lunate (4 years), scaphoid (4 to 5 years), trapezium (5
years), trapezoid (6 years), and pisiform (6 to 8 years).
The most common carpal coalition involves the lunotriquetral joint.

Embryology and Development
The arm bud is a mass of mesoderm-derived mesenchyme covered by ectoderm that
develops into the upper extremity during embryogenesis.1,2 The Hox genes regulate limb
development, and their expression is controlled by signaling proteins, such as the sonic
hedgehog fibroblast growth factor and Wnt-7a protein. The limb forms across three
anatomic axes (proximal to distal, dorsal to volar, and anterior to posterior). The arm
bud appears during week four of gestation. The forearm is separated from the upper
arm in week five of gestation. The development of digits becomes apparent at
approximately week six of gestation. During week seven of gestation, resorption of the
mesenchymal tissue between the digits occurs, causing complete separation of the
fingers and 90° rotation of the upper extremity limb along the long axis, which allows the
elbow to point dorsally. Embryogenesis is complete by week eight of gestation, with the
upper limb completely formed.1,11 Most congenital upper extremity anomalies occur
during this period of embryologic development.7

Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History and Physical Examination
During initial evaluation of patients with a congenital upper extremity anomaly, family and
medical history should be obtained. Specific inquiry with regard to the presence and
manifestation of other conditions is made.
A physical examination may include evaluation of bilateral extremities because many of these
conditions often affect both limbs.

Patient History and Physical Examination
Evaluation of a patient with congenital upper extremity anomalies should include
assessment for involvement of other organ systems. Patients may have an associated
syndrome that may necessitate coordination of a multidisciplinary team before any
surgical treatment. In addition, many conditions can have a genetic component with a
positive family history.7 The specialist should obtain a family history and consider
referrals to genetic counseling if appropriate.
Classification
Many classification schemes are available for congenital upper extremity differences.
The system devised by Swanson12 classifies conditions based on morphology and is used by
the International Federation of Societies for Surgery of the Hand (IFSSH) (Table 2).
An updated classification system called the Oberg-Manske-Tonkin classification recently was
adopted by the IFSSH13,14 based on advances in understanding of the molecular biology,
genetics, and developmental biology of limb development (Table 3).

Upper Limb–Proximal-Distal Axis
Transverse Arrest
Overview
Transverse deficiencies encompass conditions that involve complete absence of the limb
distal to a certain point on the upper extremity (Figure 1; Resource 2)
Presentation
Clinically, the extremity may appear as if it has undergone surgical amputation; however,
transverse deficiency is an embryologic failure of formation. Therefore, problems such as
bony overgrowth that are common in pediatric traumatic amputation do not occur in
congenital transverse deficiency.
The most common level is at the proximal third of the forearm
Inheritance/associations
Transverse deficiencies typically are sporadic, unilateral, and not associated with other
systemic conditions.
Transverse deficiencies typically are managed nonsurgically or with the use of prostheses.
Surgical management may be indicated if functionless parts may benefit from resection or if
stump revision may facilitate prosthetic fitting.
Although rarely used, the Krukenberg reconstruction was developed with the goal of
increasing function.
Arrest of the digits distal to the metacarpals can be managed via various surgical techniques,
including lengthening, toe phalangeal bone grafting, and toe-to-hand transfers.

Transverse Arrest
Transverse deficiencies are thought to result from disruption of the vascular supply
during embryogenesis, which causes failure of the apical ectodermal ridge.15 The
incidence of congenital transverse deficiencies has been estimated to account for 6% of
all congenital hand differences, with an incidence of approximately 1 in 20,000 live
births.14,16,17 These deficiencies typically are unilateral, without a particular sex or
genetic predisposition.18,19 Although transverse deficiencies can occur anywhere in the
upper extremity, from the finger to shoulder, the most common level is the proximal
third of the forearm.1,18 For more distal transverse deficiencies at the level of the digits,
the infant may have rudimentary nubbins.1,18 Transverse deficiencies can be
differentiated from constriction band syndrome because patients with the former

condition will have hypoplasia of the muscles proximal to the defect and children with
constriction band syndrome generally will have bands in other areas of the body as well.
Transverse deficiencies usually are managed nonsurgically; however, many surgical
techniques have been described. For transverse deficiency of the fingers distal to the
metacarpals, management may include single-stage or distraction lengthening of the
metacarpal or phalanx with distraction after an osteotomy.20,21 In addition,
nonvascularized toe phalangeal transfers21,22 and microsurgical toe-to-hand transfers
are treatment options23,24 (Video 1); however, toe transfers for congenital conditions
may be technically challenging compared with traumatic amputations because the
proximal tendons and neurovascular structures may be hypoplastic in patients with
transverse arrest.25 The functional benefit of these procedures may be limited in
children with a normally developed contralateral upper extremity.

Phocomelia is the rarest and most severe form of longitudinal deficiency.
Phocomelia is characterized by what appears to be an intercalary absence of the
limb but likely is embryologically a proximal continuum of radial or ulnar
longitudinal deficiency.
Inheritance
No known pattern of inheritance exists; however, phocomelia has been associated
with the teratogen thalidomide.
Presentation
Clinically, the limb may consist of a short hand with only three or four digits and
often an absent thumb.
Management
Management usually is nonsurgical, and surgical reconstruction has not been well
described.

Phocomelia (Intercalary Deficiency)
Occurring in approximately 1 in 125,000 live births, phocomelia is the rarest
longitudinal deficiency of the upper extremity.3,26 It also is the most severe
form of longitudinal deficiency because of absence of an intercalary segment of
the extremity. No established inheritance pattern exists; however, it has been
associated with children born to mothers taking thalidomide.27 The hand
typically has notable deformity, with only three or four digits and an absent
thumb.18,26 Goldfarb et al26 categorized this condition into three groups:
Group 1 (proximal RLD)—The proximal humerus is absent and the distal
humerus is largely maintained, articulating with the proximal ulna. The radius
is completely absent and radial dysplasia of the hand is present.
Group 2 (proximal ulnar longitudinal dysplasia)—A hypoplastic glenoid with a
single short arm or forearm bone that typically bifurcates distally is present.
The elbow joint is absent and the hand has a severe deformity typical of ulnar
dysplasia.

Group 3 (severe combined dysplasia)—Type A is characterized by absence of
the radius and ulna. Type B is characterized by total absence of the arm and
forearm and the hand is attached directly to the thorax.
Patients typically have severe functional deficits. Range of motion of the
affected extremity is limited because the lateral scapula often is deficient as
well. Management typically is nonsurgical, with devices to aid in daily activities.
Surgical management is not well described and typically is only indicated to
improve shoulder stability, create limb shortening, or facilitate thumb
opposition.15

RLD (Radial Clubhand)
Overview
RLD is failure of parts in the preaxial border of the upper extremity to form correctly.
Presentation
The radius may be deficient or completely absent, which is most common (Figure 2;
Resource 3).
The thumb and thenar muscles also usually are deficient.

RLD often is associated with various systemic conditions, including:
Thrombocytopenia absent radius—These patients typically have an absent radius, a
hypoplastic thumb, and a low platelet count at birth that normalizes over time.
Fanconi anemia—These patients have normal platelet and blood cell counts at birth but
pancytopenia develops in early childhood. Fanconi anemia may be diagnosed via a
mitomycin C or diepoxybutane chromosomal challenge test. Management consists of bone
marrow transplantation.
Holt-Oram syndrome—refers to RLD with congenital heart disease, typically atrial or
ventricular septal defects and is associated with mutations in the TBX5 gene
VACTERL syndrome—consists of vertebral anomalies, anal atresia, cardiac abnormalities,
tracheoesophageal fistula, renal agenesis, and limb defects
VATER syndrome—consists of vertebral anomalies, anal atresia, tracheoesophageal fistula,
esophageal atresia, and renal agenesis
Clinical features
Patients with RLD often exhibit elbow flexion contracture, a shortened and/or bowed
forearm, radial deviation of the wrist, and thumb aplasia or hypoplasia.

In addition to skeletal deficiencies, similar deficiencies of soft-tissue structures, such as the
radial artery, median nerve, and flexor carpi radialis, may be observed.
The Bayne and Klug classification system is commonly used to characterize the severity of
RLD into four types,30 which has since been modified by other authors.31 The original types
are as follows:
Type I (short distal radius)—The distal radius epiphysis is deficient, resulting in a mildly
shortened radius; the thumb is hypoplastic with adequate carpal support.
Type II (hypoplastic radius)—Proximal and distal radial epiphyses are deficient, the radius is
substantially shortened, bowing of the ulna is present, and the carpus is poorly supported.
Type III (partial absence of the radius)—The proximal, middle, or distal third of the radius is
absent; absence of the distal radius is most common; bowing of the ulna is present; and
the carpus is poorly supported.
Type IV (total absence of the radius)—The radius is completely absent; the hand is
unsupported and is severely displaced radially; this is the most common type of radial
deficiency.
Management
Splint and/or serial cast immobilization are initiated early in infancy to stretch the tight
radial soft tissues.
Surgical treatment options include soft-tissue procedures and bony procedures, such as
centralization (the axis of the ulna is realigned with the long metacarpal) or radialization
(the ulna is realigned with the index metacarpal). Both methods often use previous soft-
tissue distraction to enhance outcomes.
Despite initial improvements in alignment, the main complication of RLD surgery is
recurrence of deformity. In addition, overzealous attempts at deformity correction may
lead to growth arrest of the distal ulnar physis.
Surgical management is not recommended in patients with elbow stiffness or in older
patients who have compensated for/adjusted to their deficiency.

RLD (Radial Clubhand)
RLD, previously referred to as radial clubhand or radial ray deficiency, involves failure
of formation along the preaxial or radial border of the upper extremity. The thumb,
thenar musculature, and radius usually are involved.28,29 This condition has been

reported to occur in as many as 1 in 50,000 live births, and 50% of cases are
bilateral.1,3,18,27
The patient must undergo evaluation of the other systems commonly involved with
radial deficiency, especially the cardiac, renal, and hematologic systems. The
syndromes classically associated with this condition include Holt-Oram syndrome, an
autosomal dominant condition that often involves cardiac septal defects;
thrombocytopenia absent radius syndrome, an autosomal recessive condition
characterized by thrombocytopenia and a present thumb; Fanconi anemia, an
autosomal recessive condition that includes aplastic anemia that manifests itself at
age 6 years and is fatal without a bone marrow transplant; VACTERL syndrome, which
involves vertebral anomalies, anal atresia, cardiac abnormalities, tracheoesophageal
fistula, renal agenesis, and limb defects; and VATER syndrome, which involves
vertebral anomalies, anal atresia, cardiac abnormalities, tracheoesophageal fistula,
renal agenesis, and limb defects.28 Chromosomal analyses may be required for
diagnosis, and coordination of care with the patient’s pediatrician and subspecialists
is necessary.
Because the hand often is poorly supported and in a flexed and radially deviated
position, poor tendon excursion is present and, as a result, poor function of the limb
is noted. Nonsurgical management should begin immediately after birth via passive
stretching and serial splint/cast immobilization to centralize the hand onto the wrist.
Often, an elbow extension contracture is present and also should be managed via
stretching.1,32 Surgical management is performed between ages 6 and 24 months,
and centralization of the carpus on the remaining ulna traditionally has been the
mainstay of management. This procedure usually involves tendon transfers to correct
the radial deformation forces, and corrective osteotomies may be required if
considerable ulnar bowing is present.33-34 However, more surgeons are performing
soft-tissue reconstruction to prevent any injury to the distal ulna physis.35 Because
the thumb may have severe hypoplasia in radial clubhand, a pollicization procedure in
the first year of life also may be indicated.36, 37 Surgical treatment is contraindicated
in older patients who have adapted to their deformity and are happy with their
function and patients with marked elbow contractures who depend on their radially
deviated wrist to perform activities. In addition, surgical treatment may be deferred in

Ulnar Longitudinal Deficiency (Ulnar Clubhand)
Overview
Ulnar longitudinal deficiency (ULD) is failure of formation of parts in the postaxial border of
the upper extremity.
ULD is 5 to 10 times less common than RLD.3
Inheritance/associations
Ulnar deficiency occurs sporadically, with rare autosomal dominant inheritance patterns, and
it is not associated with the numerous medical conditions observed in patients with RLD.
A strong association exists with musculoskeletal manifestations, such as scoliosis, proximal
femoral focal deficiency, and fibular deficiency.
Presentation
Patients may present on a spectrum of ular deficiencies, from involvement of the hand only
to total absence of the ulna and radiohumeral synostosis (Figure 3).
Dissimilar from radial deficiency, the wrist is stable in ulnar deficiency.
Management
Nonsurgical management includes stretching and serial cast/splint immobilization.
Surgical management generally is focused on the associated hand differences and includes
syndactyly releases and derotational osteotomies of the digits.
Occasionally, excision of a fibrous ulnar anlage allows for more normal growth of the radius
in patients with a shortened or absent ulna.

Ulnar Longitudinal Deficiency (Ulnar Clubhand)
Previously referred to as ulnar clubhand or ulnar dysmelia, ULD involves failure of
formation along the postaxial or ulnar border of the upper extremity.38 It is much more
rare than radial deficiency, only occurring in approximately 1 in 25,000 live births.3 In
addition, ULD occurs sporadically, and it is not associated with the systemic medical

present with other musculoskeletal anomalies, such as proximal femoral focal
deficiency, fibular deficiency, congenital scoliosis, and phocomelia.1,40Patients may
present with a spectrum of deficiencies on the ulnar side of the hand and forearm.
Usually, ulnar deficiency occurs unilaterally in the upper extremity with hypoplasia of the
entire limb.40 The forearm usually is shortened and has a bowed apex radially. Radial
head dislocation is common, and the elbow may be fused via radiohumeral
synostosis.41,42 Often, an anlage of fibrous tissue is present that replaces the deficient
ulna. Dissimilar from radial deficiency, the wrist usually is stable. Digital anomalies are
present in approximately 90% of patients. In addition, thumb and first web space
abnormalities occur in more than 70% of patients. Syndactyly also is common, occurring
in approximately 30% of patients.40,42
Many classification systems for ULD exist. Bayne43 categorized this condition based on
the status of the forearm and elbow, with Havenhill et al44 and Goldfarb et al26 adding
type 0 and type V, respectively.
Type 0: normal ulna, normal radius, stable elbow, and digital hypoplasia or absence
with carpal coalition or absence
Type I: hypoplastic ulna with distal and proximal epiphyses present, mild radial
bowing, stable elbow, and mild ulnar deviation of the wrist with digital hypoplasia or
absence
Type II: partial ulnar aplasia with the proximal ulna present and an anlage that tethers
the radius, radial bowing, variable elbow stability with possible posterolateral
dislocation of the radial head, and mild ulnar deviation of the wrist
Type III: total absence of the ulna without anlage, straight radius, elbow instability with
posterolateral dislocation of the radial head and possible severe elbow flexion
deformity, less ulnar deviation of the wrist, and severe deficiencies of the carpus
bones and digits
Type IV: usually total absence of the ulna with anlage present, radiohumeral
synostosis with internal rotation of the humerus and forearm pronation, and ulnar
deviation of the wrist
Type V: total absence of the ulna, straight radius, radiohumeral synostosis and
humeral bifurcation or a large medial condyle, less ulnar deviation of the wrist, and

Because management of ulnar deficiency primarily is driven by restoration of hand
function, classification of this condition based on the status of the thumb may have
greater clinical importance. The classification system described by Cole and Manske45
commonly is used:
Type A: normal first web space and thumb
Type B: mild first web space and thumb deficiency
Type C: moderate to severe first web space and thumb deficiencies, potential loss of
thumb opposition, malrotation of the thumb into the plane of other digits, thumb to
index finger syndactyly, and absent extrinsic tendon function
Type D: absent thumb
Nonsurgical management of ULD includes serial cast and splint immobilization
beginning shortly after birth.18 Surgical management of the hand may include syndactyly
release, first web space deepening, and derotational osteotomies of the first
metacarpal.42,45 Excision of the ulnar anlage typically is indicated to prevent progression
of radial bowing.40,46 For patients with severe radial bowing, a radial osteotomy may be
required. If a radial head dislocation is substantially limiting elbow extension, then radial
head resection and creation of a one-bone forearm may be considered; however, the
presence of a proximal ulnar fragment is required.18,37
Madelung Deformity (Figure 4)
Madelung deformity is a defect of the volar ulnar aspect of the distal radial physis leading to
progressive volar tilt and radial displacement of the hand.
One proposed mechanism includes tethering of the Vickers ligament.
Most commonly presents in females.
Autosomal inheritance has been described, with an association to Leri-Weill
dyschondrosteosis, but more often it is idiopathic. Symptoms typically manifest in adolescence
with progressive volar displacement of the hand leading to ulnar impaction and limited wrist
motion.

For patients with progressive deformity and severe symptoms, surgical release of the Vickers

Madelung Deformity
Madelung deformity is characterized by a dyschondrosis of the volar ulnar aspect of the
distal radial physis. Because partial deficiency of growth is present in this area, patients

will have progressive volar tilt and radial inclination.48 It most commonly presents in
adolescent females, and it is associated with Leri-Weill dyschondrosteosis, which is a
form of mesomelic dwarfism.48 One cause of the deformity is thought to be tethering of
the Vickers ligament, which may limit growth at the volar ulnar aspect of the physis.49
The Vickers ligament is a fibrous band running from the distal radius to the lunate on the

Symphalangism is the failure of development of the interphalangeal joints.116 Although
the proximal interphalangeal joint and the distal interphalangeal joint may be involved,
proximal symphalangism is more common, and patients present with fused proximal

dominant manner.118 Symphalangism is associated with systemic conditions, such as
Apert syndrome, Poland syndrome, and conductive hearing loss. It also may present
with other musculoskeletal anomalies, such as syndactyly, radiohumeral fusion, carpal
synostosis, tarsal coalition, congenital cervical spine fusion, and symphalangism of the
toes.117-120 Symphalangism has been classified by Flatt and Wood118 as true
symphalangism with no other skeletal anomalies, symphalangism associated with
symbrachydactyly, and symphalangism associated with syndactyly. Patients lack active
and passive joint motion and absent skin creases at the joints. The ulnar fingers are
more commonly affected, and patients often have some flexion because of normally
developed metacarpophalangeal and distal interphalangeal joints. Surgical management
usually is not required because the functional loss from the fused phalanges often is not
severe. Described surgical techniques include interphalangeal joint arthroplasty and
osteotomy with fusion of the proximal interphalangeal joint at 45° to improve grasp;
however, surgical outcomes have been reported to have limited success.1,117,121

Overview
Amniotic band syndrome also is referred to as constriction ring syndrome or amniotic

Amniotic band syndrome is thought to be sporadic, without hereditary predisposition.

Amniotic Band Syndrome
Amniotic band syndrome also is known as congenital constriction ring syndrome, in
which constriction rings may circumferentially wrap around digits or an entire limb in
utero.131 It occurs in approximately 1 in 15,000 live births.132 It is believed to be
sporadic, without evidence of inheritance. A proposed intrinsic mechanism has
suggested that the anomalies and fibrous bands share a common origin, caused by
disruption of the developing germinal disc during embryogenesis.133 The most widely
accepted theory involves an extrinsic mechanism, in which disruption in the amnion
releases fibrous strands of membrane that encircle the limbs of the developing fetus,
leading to vascular and lymphatic compromise.134 This condition frequently is
associated with other congenital anomalies, such as syndactyly, hypoplasia,
symphalangism, clubfoot, cleft lip and palate, and craniofacial defects.135,136 Most cases
occur in the hand and the index, long, and ring fingers are affected more often than the
border digits. The bands typically occur transversely, or perpendicular to the long axis of

presenting in a mild groove typically in a transverse fashion; type II, in which the ring is
deeper and deformity is distal to the ring, usually lymphoma or hypoplasia; type III, in
which fusion is distal to the ring with syndactyly; and type IV, in which complete
amputation is distal to the ring.
Management depends on severity of presentation. For type I, observation is adequate.
Occasionally, surgical release of the constriction ring may be performed to improve
cosmesis. Ring excision typically is the treatment option for type II, and the defect is
closed via Z-plasty, W-plasty, or V-Y flaps. Simple excision of the ring alone would be
insufficient because it may lead to circumferential scar contracture. Syndactyly
reconstruction is indicated for type III conditions, with release of the border digits at
approximately age 6 months, followed by the central digits later.
Often, amputations in type IV constriction band syndrome have adequate soft-tissue
coverage and may not require surgical management; however, reconstruction
occasionally may improve function with procedures such as osseous lengthening,
deepening of web spaces, and toe-to-hand transfers.131 In general, toe-to-hand transfers
are performed at the ulnar digits to allow a pincer motion.137 In addition, on-top plasty,
or partial digital transfer, may be performed. This may be indicated if the index
metacarpal is removed during a first web space deepening procedure to build onto a
thumb stump or if a partially amputated index or ring finger is transferred to the distal
end of an amputated long finger.131

Macrodactyly
Macrodactyly is a congenital deformity in which all components of a digit or digits are
increased in size.139 This condition is rare, composing approximately 1% of all upper
extremity congenital abnormalities and occurring in approximately 1 in 100,000 live
births.140 Most cases are sporadic and appear in isolation; however, it also may be
associated with syndactyly and syndromes such as neurofibromatosis and Klippel-
Trènaunay-Weber syndrome, a condition characterized by extremity hypertrophy,
hemangiomas, and varicose veins.141-143 Two categories of macrodactyly include the
static form and the progressive form.139 For static macrodactyly, the deformity is
present at birth, and the involved finger grows in proportion to the other unaffected
fingers. Outcomes for patients with this static form are predictably better than those of
patients with the progressive form.141 The progressive condition is more common, and it
manifests in childhood, at which time the affected fingers will enlarge in an unrestricted
manner disproportionately relative to the other fingers until skeletal maturity.7,139 For a
digit exhibiting progressive growth, staged surgical debulking typically is required.
Physeal arrest can be performed to limit longitudinal growth after the affected digit
reaches expected adult length.141 Digital shortening via osteotomy and phalangectomy
also have been described.144,145 For severely affected digits not amenable to
reconstruction, amputation may be indicated.141

Camptodactyly consists of a flexion deformity of the proximal interphalangeal joint,
usually the little finger; however, other digits may be affected. This occurs in less than 1%
of the population, and most patients are asymptomatic.146 It may be sporadic or have
autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance.147 Presentation may be
unilateral or bilateral.148,149 Multiple etiologies have been suggested, including
attenuated or absent FDS and/or profundus tendons and abnormal lumbrical insertion.

occurs in isolation and in the little finger. Type II deformity also is known as the acquired

may progress to a severe flexion deformity with the proximal interphalangeal joint
becoming flexed 90°.153 Type III deformity occurs in patients with an underlying
syndrome, most commonly arthrogryposis. Multiple digits often are involved bilaterally;
however, the severity is usually asymmetric.4

options include stretching, serial splinting, and serial cast immobilization. These
treatment options can be used for all patients but are particularly recommended for
patients with flexion deformities less than 60°.155 Dynamic splinting is associated with
good results; however, contracture may recur after discontinuation of splinting.156

deformity.157,158 Surgical management may be considered after failed nonsurgical
treatment in patients with a flexion deformity greater than 60°, and it should be
individualized to manage the underlying pathologic condition of the patient.149,159 For
deformities that are passively correctable, soft-tissue releases of the volar skin with flap,
fascia, and volar plate may be considered in combination with FDS tenotomy or transfer
to the lateral bands or the extensor apparatus.160,161 For fixed deformity, osteotomy
and fusion also may be considered.154
